title: Against Curriculum Dilution (and What To Do Instead) Education Caracappa, Michele
author: Caracappa, Michele
summary: Caracappa draws on a March 2026 Kappan piece and a RAND study to examine why teachers routinely reduce the rigor of high-quality instructional materials (HQIM) -- a phenomenon researchers call curriculum dilution. She distinguishes between dilution (teachers simplifying tasks because they doubt students can handle them) and the legitimate critique that even 'all-green' EdReports curricula have real quality gaps. The research from Jackson et al. shows that teachers who maintained high expectations found ways to support students without reducing cognitive demand, while those who doubted students lowered the bar. Caracappa argues for curriculum fortification: a dual commitment to developing teachers' capacity to implement materials with fidelity and to openly improving the curriculum itself where it falls short. She proposes collaborative professional learning structures -- student-work protocols, inclusive professional learning with specialists, and collective sense-making -- as the institutional moves that build both teacher efficacy and student access to grade-level content.
points: Curriculum dilution is not a character flaw in teachers but a rational response to being asked to teach grade-level materials to students multiple grades behind -- the systemic conditions, not individual teachers, drive the behavior.

The 'all-green on EdReports' gold standard is a poor proxy for actual quality: standards alignment does not capture evidence of efficacy, cultural responsiveness, text complexity, or whether the curriculum actually builds knowledge.

Teachers who maintain high expectations explain student difficulty through the lens of their own instruction rather than student deficit -- a key distinction that research links to higher cognitive demand in practice.

Curriculum fortification goes beyond fidelity: it requires creating school forums where teachers can name curriculum limitations, share purposeful adaptations, and collectively agree on enrichments that raise quality for all students.

Protocols for looking at student work that frame student output as a signal for instructional shifts -- rather than as evidence of student deficit -- can create virtuous cycles where teacher efficacy and student success reinforce each other.
quotes: RAND found that nearly all teachers alter HQIM content in ways that undermine coherence. Researchers have coined the term curriculum dilution to describe this quiet but pervasive trimming, simplifying, and supplementing that reduces rigor and disrupts instructional design.

David Steiner asks: 'If you were a teacher faced with twenty-five thirteen-year-olds whose knowledge of math and ELA ranged from one to three years below grade level, would you readily teach materials that assumed grade-level competence?' He reinforces the rational nature of decision-making that results in dilution.

Low expectations are not distributed at random -- but rather reflect societal biases and inequities that reinforce deficit perspectives around marginalized students' capabilities as learners. Dr. Sonja Santelises calls this 'educational redlining.'

Teachers who maintained a belief in their students' capabilities found ways to adjust curriculum while '[maintaining] the cognitive demand of high level tasks.' They viewed their students' current struggles with grade-level mastery as a temporary rather than permanent condition.

There's now far more clarity in the field that standards-alignment is a poor proxy for quality. Compare several 'all green' curricula on EdReports and you're likely to find wild variability when it comes to everything from actual evidence of efficacy, to cultural responsiveness and inclusivity.

Curriculum fortification is not only an opportunity to ensure teachers have the tools and capacity to support all of their students in grappling with a curriculum as written. It's also an opportunity to address gaps and improve upon the curriculum itself.
Teachers know and understand this and many were waving their hands to call attention to these issues far before many of their system leaders responsible for purchasing decisions were taking notice.
